course_description:
An introduction to screen studies which explores the relationship between film and television and provides techniques for analysing screen texts, understanding the industrial and institutional history of film and television, and exploring the impact of aesthetic style, stardom, and genre on meaning and audience responses.

Introduction to Film and Television Studies is designed to teach students how to carefully observe, closely analyse, and critically evaluate films and TV programs. Students are introduced to fundamental concepts of form and storytelling, before moving on to closely examining different elements of style. The final portion of the course introduces students to "big picture" ideas: truth and fiction, the idea of film as a medium, authorship, and genre and criticism. Screenings come from a range of historical periods, cultural contexts, genres, and forms.

course_aims: Students completing this course will have acquired the analytical and research skills needed to pursue further study in the field of film and television studies.ﾠ Questions to be addressed by the course include: How does the formal organisation of a film or television program (i.e., its technical, aesthetic, and narrative conventions) contribute to the way viewers think about and engage with it?ﾠ How can we account for both similarities and differences in the way that individual viewers respond to the same text?

learning_outcomes.description: Explain and apply the technical and analytical terms used in relation to film and television
Use the language of film and television criticism and analysis in effective written and verbal communication.
Critically analyse films and television programs
Demonstrate an understanding of the industrial and institutional contexts of film and television production and reception.
Apply the skills of film and television analysis to a variety of research problems and critical approaches in screen studies and adjacent disciplines.
Build upon your introduction to and further develop your familiarity with films and television programs of different nations, cultures, and languages.

assessment_details.title: In-Tutorial Writing Exercises
assessment_details.due_date: Week 2 - Week 8 Week 10 - Week 13 Due in your tutorial each week.
assessment_details.task_description: Each week in your assigned tutorial, starting in week 2, there will be a timed writing exercise that must be completed on the provided sheet. You are responsible for bringing your own pen or pencil. Responses must be handwritten unless there is an accessibility requirement. You are not permitted to access electronic devices of any kind during the writing exercise. You may consult printed or handwritten notes. You must sign the attendance sheet in your tutorial within the first thirty minutes of your tutorial commencing in order to complete the In-Tutorial Exercise for that week. There are 10 total exercises , each is worth 3 marks . You will receive 3 marks for each complete response, 1.5 marks for a partial answer, and zero marks for responses that are incorrect or incomplete (whether unsubmitted because of non-attendance, submitted but blank, submitted but not responding to the prompt, illegible, etc.). If you have not followed an instruction to put away your device, you will be referred to an Integrity Officer for investigation. Content Tasks (Week 2; 4-8): For 6 weeks, you will be given a specific prompt for each exercise that will refer to content from that week’s topic. The question may be related to a still image or brief clip presented in tutorial. Feedback will be given informally via peer groups in the tutorial immediately after writing. A running total of your marks will be released part-way through semester, and your final marks will be released on blackboard during or shortly after the final teaching week. Please do not request marks from your tutor or course coordinator on an ad hoc basis. Process Notes (Week 10-13) In the final 4 tutorials, you will complete a series of writing exercises related to the final essay. These exercises are designed to help you conceptualise, plan, and develop your essay. Submission of 2 out of 4 of the Process Notes tasks is a hurdle requirement to pass the Final Essay assessment. This means that if you complete fewer than 2 of the process notes exercises in class you will not be eligible to pass the Final Essay, regardless of the quality of your submission. Students who do not meet the hurdle requirement will receive a maximum of 49% for the assessment item. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Audio Commentary (Sample Annotations; Recorded Commentary + Transcript)
assessment_details.task_description: You are required to produce an audio commentary over one of the Commentary Clips listed in the Assessment Booklet (also posted on Blackboard). Each of the clips comes from the opening sequence of a Set Screening. It is strongly recommended that you watch the entire film that contains the clip you will be using. You are required to offer a structured, analytical commentary that explains how and why formal and/or stylistic choices shape the sequence to create meaning, deliver some sort of effect, or guide the viewer’s attention; you must make some point about why the scene you are analysing is important in the way it sets up the rest of the film. You are to download your chosen clip from Blackboard, record your audio commentary and add it to the clip. You will submit this separately from the transcript – there will be individual links on Blackboard for each component of your submission. Please see the Audio Commentary Resources section in the Assessment Booklet to help navigate the technological requirements of this piece of assessment. There are two (2) parts to this assessment: Part A: Sample Annotations (submitted in-person to your tutor in week 6 tutorial) [see hurdle information] Part B: Clip with Commentary + Written Transcript Part A: Sample Annotations (submitted in-person to your tutor in week 6 tutorial) In the week 6 tutorial, you will submit a hard copy of handwritten, informal, sample annotations of your chosen clip, accompanying 3-5 shots from that clip. You should not aim to provide exhaustive detail of every aspect of style and form. Instead, your notes should be indicative of your thinking to show the elements of style/form you have selected, a couple of examples of how they are working in some key moments, and what it is they achieve. An exemplar of this is available on Blackboard, as is a template. Part A (Sample Annotations) does not contribute to the mark you will receive for this piece of assessment. Your tutor will provide general feedback in the tutorial in week 7 to the class as a whole to help you develop your final submission. Part B: Clip with Commentary + Transcript (Transcript: 600-800 words inclusive of all referencing and formatting requirements) This assessment is designed to evaluate your ability to select, analyse, and explain the significance of particular stylistic and formal features in a given clip. It is not a play-by-play of plot, nor is it a comprehensive account of every aspect of style and form present in the clip. You are also not pretending to be the director (and so not inventing production stories and the like). Instead, you should speak as an informed analyst explaining how the film works. There will be an exemplar on Blackboard for you to watch and listen to. Your commentary should demonstrate your understanding of film form and style (using technical terminology from Film Art across relevant aspects of mise-en-scene/cinematography/editing/sound) as well as your capacity to make a reasonable case for the plausible intended effects of artistic decisions involving film form and style. This means that you should have a clear point you are trying to convey via your analysis, a clear rationale for the features you are focusing on, and a sense of how the different features are working together. It is important that you prioritise depth over breadth: do not try to cover every single feature, do not make general claims, do not make assertions without any kind of evidence through analysis, do not merely describe what happens on screen. It is important to identify relevant techniques, but you need to go to the next step and explain what they do and why they are important. It is also critical that you make some claim about how your chosen scene sets up the film as a whole – that you offer an informed and reasonable suggestion of the importance of the style and/or form you focus on to the way the film unfolds. Please consult the exemplar on Blackboard. You only need to refer to Film Art as shown in the transcript exemplar on Blackboard – production trivia and scholarly sources will negatively impact your work. Focus on your own original insight and analysis of the clip. Please Note: The film you analyse for this piece of assessment cannot be analysed in your Final Essay. assessment_details.title: Final Essay (Process Notes; Comparative Analysis Essay)
assessment_details.task_description: Your task is to write an essay wherein you make an argument via the analysis of your clips in response to your chosen question, supported by an appropriate use of scholarly material. Your analysis should take into account relevant stylistic and formal features of your chosen clips. The features that are relevant will depend on the argument you are making, and the argument itself should involve a coherent and sensible rationale for the clips that you are comparing. It is important that your essay responds clearly to your chosen question. There are two (2) parts to this assessment: Part A: Process Notes [see hurdle information] Part B: Comparative Analysis Essay Process Notes : In tutorials, you will complete a series of writing exercises related to conceptualising your essay. These are marked as part of the "weekly tutorial writing task" series, but are a hurdle requirement for the final essay -- you must submit 2/4 of these tasks in-person to pass the essay. The word count does not apply to the process notes. Comparative Analysis Essay Full details are provided in the Assessment Booklet. Read full task description Hide full task description

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
